content.text: For most of human history, people believed the universe was static and unchanging, a fixed stage on which stars and planets played out their roles. This view was so deeply held that even Albert Einstein, when his equations of general relativity predicted a dynamic universe, introduced a "cosmological constant" to force a static solution. He later called this his greatest blunder.

The discovery that the universe is expanding was one of the most profound breakthroughs in the history of science. It changed our understanding of the cosmos and led to the Big Bang theory, which describes how the entire observable universe began from an incredibly hot, dense state approximately 13.8 billion years ago.

In this lesson, we will explore the evidence for the expanding universe, starting with the Doppler effect and redshift, moving through Hubble's law, and examining the Big Bang theory and the evidence that supports it. We will also consider what the expansion means for the future of the universe.
Before we can understand the evidence for an expanding universe, we need to understand the

. You have probably experienced the Doppler effect with sound: when an ambulance approaches you, its siren sounds higher-pitched, and when it moves away, the siren sounds lower-pitched. This happens because the motion of the source compresses the sound waves in front of it (shorter wavelength, higher frequency) and stretches them behind it (longer wavelength, lower frequency).
The same principle applies to light. Light is an electromagnetic wave, and if a light source is moving relative to an observer, the wavelength of the light is shifted:
the observer, the light waves are compressed, shifting the light towards shorter wavelengths (the blue end of the visible spectrum).
from the observer, the light waves are stretched, shifting the light towards longer wavelengths (the red end of the visible spectrum).
The amount of redshift or blueshift depends on the speed of the source relative to the observer. A faster-moving source produces a greater shift.

How We Detect Redshift in Starlight

Every chemical element produces a unique pattern of spectral lines, specific wavelengths of light that the element absorbs or emits. These patterns act like fingerprints, allowing astronomers to identify which elements are present in a star or galaxy.

When astronomers observe the light from a distant galaxy, they can identify these spectral line patterns, but they find that the entire pattern is shifted towards longer wavelengths (towards the red end of the spectrum). The pattern is still recognisable, so the elements can still be identified, but every line has been shifted by the same fractional amount. This is redshift, and it tells us that the galaxy is moving away from us.

An important point to understand is that it is not the galaxies themselves that are flying through space. Rather, it is

. The galaxies are being carried along as the fabric of space stretches. A common analogy is dots drawn on the surface of a balloon. As the balloon inflates, all the dots move apart from each other, and dots that are farther apart move apart faster. No dot is at the "centre" of the expansion; every dot sees every other dot moving away.
This means there is no centre of the universe. Every point in the universe sees every other point receding from it, which is exactly what we observe.

Estimating the Age of the Universe from Hubble's Law

Hubble's law provides a way to estimate the age of the universe. If galaxies are moving apart now, they must have been closer together in the past. If we run the expansion backwards, all the matter in the universe would converge to a single point. The time it would take for this to happen gives an estimate of the age of the universe. The observation that the universe is expanding naturally leads to a remarkable conclusion: if we trace the expansion backwards in time, the universe must have been smaller, denser, and hotter in the past. Taken to its logical extreme, this means that at some point in the distant past, all the matter and energy in the universe were concentrated in an incredibly hot, incredibly dense state. The event that marks the beginning of the expansion of the universe from this state is called the
The Big Bang theory states that:
The universe began approximately 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state.
Space itself has been expanding ever since, carrying matter and radiation with it.
As the universe expanded, it cooled, allowing particles to form, then atoms, then eventually stars and galaxies.
It is important to understand what the Big Bang was
It was not an explosion in space (like a bomb going off). Rather, it was an expansion
It did not happen at a particular location in the universe. The Big Bang happened everywhere at once, because at the beginning, everywhere was the same place.
The Big Bang theory does not explain what caused the Big Bang or what existed "before" it. The concept of "before" may not even be meaningful if time itself began with the Big Bang.
Timeline of the Universe After the Big Bang
The history of the universe after the Big Bang can be summarised as follows:
The Big Bang. The universe is infinitely hot and dense (as far as our current physics can describe).
Fundamental particles (quarks, electrons, neutrinos) form. The universe is a hot, dense soup of particles and radiation.
The universe has cooled enough for protons and neutrons to combine into the nuclei of light elements: hydrogen, helium, and traces of lithium. This process is called

The universe has cooled to about 3,000 K. Electrons combine with nuclei to form neutral atoms. The universe becomes transparent to light for the first time. The radiation released at this time is what we now observe as the cosmic microwave background radiation.
The first stars begin to form from clouds of hydrogen and helium gas.

As discussed above, the observation that almost all galaxies are moving away from us (showing redshift) and that more distant galaxies are moving away faster is exactly what we would expect if the universe is expanding from an initial hot, dense state. This was the first major piece of evidence for the Big Bang.

is perhaps the most compelling piece of evidence for the Big Bang theory. It was predicted theoretically in 1948 and accidentally discovered in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, who were working with a radio antenna at Bell Laboratories in New Jersey, USA.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough for atoms to form and for the universe to become transparent to electromagnetic radiation. The radiation that was released at that moment has been travelling through space ever since, but as the universe has expanded, the wavelength of this radiation has been stretched enormously. What was once high-energy visible light and ultraviolet radiation has been redshifted into the microwave part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

The discovery of the CMBR provided powerful confirmation of the Big Bang theory. No other theory of the origin of the universe has been able to explain the existence and properties of the CMBR as successfully.

As our understanding of the universe has deepened, two major puzzles have emerged that challenge our picture of the cosmos.

When astronomers study the rotation of galaxies, they find that stars in the outer regions of galaxies are orbiting much faster than expected. Based on the visible matter alone, the gravitational force should be too weak to keep these outer stars in their orbits; they should fly off into space. The fact that they do not means there must be additional mass that we cannot see.

of the total mass-energy content of the universe. By contrast, ordinary matter (the atoms that make up stars, planets, and people) accounts for only about

The nature of dark matter remains one of the greatest unsolved problems in physics. Various candidates have been proposed, including hypothetical particles called WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles), but dark matter has not yet been directly detected in a laboratory.
In 1998, two teams of astronomers made a startling discovery while studying distant supernovae: the expansion of the universe is not slowing down, as everyone expected. Instead, the expansion is
. Something is pushing the universe apart at an ever-increasing rate.

of the total mass-energy content of the universe.

The nature of dark energy is even more mysterious than dark matter. It could be a property of space itself (related to Einstein's cosmological constant), or it could be a new form of energy that fills the universe. Understanding dark energy is one of the biggest challenges facing modern physics.
To summarise the composition of the universe:

| Component | Percentage of total mass-energy |
|---|---|
| Dark energy | ~68% |
| Dark matter | ~27% |
| Ordinary matter | ~5% |

This means that everything we can see, every star, planet, gas cloud, and living thing, makes up less than 5% of the universe. The remaining 95% is composed of dark matter and dark energy, which we can detect only through their gravitational and cosmological effects.

What will happen to the universe in the distant future? This depends on the balance between the expansion of the universe and the gravitational attraction of all the matter within it. There are three main possibilities, often described by the geometry of the universe:

If the density of matter and energy in the universe is too low to halt the expansion, the universe will continue expanding forever, and the rate of expansion will never reverse. Over time, stars will exhaust their fuel, galaxies will fade, and the universe will become a cold, dark, empty place. This scenario is sometimes called the
of the universe. In an open universe, space has a negative curvature (like a saddle shape).

If the density of matter and energy is high enough, gravity will eventually overcome the expansion and pull everything back together. The universe would stop expanding, begin contracting, and eventually collapse back into an extremely hot, dense state, sometimes called the
This would be the reverse of the Big Bang. In a closed universe, space has a positive curvature (like the surface of a sphere).

If the density is at exactly the critical value, the expansion will slow down over time and asymptotically approach zero, but never quite stop. This is the boundary case between the open and closed universes. In a flat universe, space has zero curvature (like a flat sheet).
Current observations, including measurements of the CMBR by satellites such as WMAP and Planck, suggest that the universe is very close to

. However, the discovery of dark energy complicates this picture: the accelerating expansion driven by dark energy suggests that the universe will continue expanding forever, with the rate of expansion increasing over time. This means the most likely future scenario is the Big Freeze, with galaxies eventually becoming isolated from each other as the space between them expands faster than light can travel across it.

Misconception 1: "The Big Bang was an explosion in space"

The Big Bang was not an explosion that occurred at a particular point in space, flinging matter outward into a pre-existing void. Rather, it was the rapid expansion of space itself. Every point in the universe was the site of the Big Bang. There is no centre of the expansion and no edge to expand into.
Misconception 2: "Galaxies are moving through space away from us"

While it is common to describe galaxies as "moving away," it is more accurate to say that the space between galaxies is expanding. The galaxies themselves are not flying through space like bullets; they are being carried apart by the stretching of space. This distinction becomes important at very large distances, where the apparent recessional speed can exceed the speed of light (which would be impossible for objects moving through space but is perfectly allowed for the expansion of space itself).
Misconception 3: "Redshift means the light is red"

Redshift does not mean the light appears red. It means the wavelength has been shifted towards longer wavelengths (towards the red end of the spectrum). A blue spectral line that is redshifted might still appear blue; it has just moved to a slightly longer wavelength than it would have without the redshift. Similarly, some redshifted light may be shifted out of the visible spectrum entirely into the infrared.
Misconception 4: "The universe is expanding into something"

The universe is not expanding into pre-existing empty space. As far as we know, the universe is all there is. The expansion means that the distances between objects within the universe are increasing. This is difficult to visualise because our everyday experience does not include the stretching of space, but the mathematics and observations are clear.
Misconception 5: "The Big Bang theory is just a guess"

The Big Bang theory is supported by multiple independent lines of strong evidence: the expansion of the universe (galactic redshift), the cosmic microwave background radiation, the observed abundances of light elements, and the observed large-scale structure of the universe. While there are still open questions, the Big Bang theory is one of the best-supported theories in all of science.

The cosmic microwave background radiation (CMBR) is thermal radiation left over from the early universe. About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe had cooled enough for atoms to form and for space to become transparent to electromagnetic radiation. The radiation released at that time has been travelling through space ever since, but has been stretched by the expansion of the universe from visible/ultraviolet light into microwaves.

), the recessional velocity of a galaxy is directly proportional to its distance. More distant galaxies are moving away from us faster because the space between us and them is expanding at a greater total rate (more space means more cumulative expansion). Since a greater recessional velocity produces a greater Doppler shift, more distant galaxies show a greater redshift.

A greater redshift means a greater recessional velocity (the galaxy is moving away from us faster). By Hubble's law, since recessional velocity is proportional to distance, the galaxy with the greater redshift is also farther away. Therefore, the first galaxy is both moving away faster and is at a greater distance than the second galaxy.

When we say space itself is expanding, we mean that the distances between galaxies are increasing because the fabric of space is stretching, not because galaxies are flying through a fixed space like projectiles. A useful analogy is dots drawn on the surface of a balloon: as the balloon inflates, every dot moves away from every other dot, with more distant dots separating faster. No dot is at the centre of the expansion. This is different from an explosion in space, where objects would be moving through pre-existing space from a central point. The expansion of space also explains why very distant galaxies can appear to recede faster than the speed of light, which would be impossible for objects moving through space but is allowed for the expansion of space itself.
